headline: High: Aider can write and commit shared repo state while Plane can ingest files and broad network egress creates leakage and workflow-conflict risks; prompt-injection is lower but present via shared files.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: Aider reads and writes git-tracked files and can execute shell commands, so malicious content in shared repo files could influence its prompts or edits. Plane can ingest files and hyperlinks, creating a plausible bridge if Aider-generated artifacts are later imported. The pair lacks explicit provenance controls, so the interaction is plausible though not directly documented.
conditions: IF Plane imports Aider-authored files into task notes or issue descriptions
IF Aider is pointed at a repository containing attacker-controlled markdown or prompt text
mitigations: Restrict shared repo folders to trusted contributors only
Review imported file contents before Plane ingestion
Use a separate staging directory for Aider outputs
Add a manual approval step before copying text between tools

B_data_leakage.rationale: Aider touches source code, git history, and model-provider APIs, while Plane handles files, notes, and hyperlinks. If the same workspace contains secrets or sensitive code, Aider may send context to external model providers and Plane may store or expose uploaded files. The profiles show a plausible shared-data path, but no direct evidence of a mandatory leak.
conditions: IF sensitive source code or secrets are present in the shared repository
IF Plane file uploads include confidential documents or screenshots
mitigations: Exclude secrets from the shared repo
Disable uploads of confidential files into Plane
Use redacted snippets when sending code to Aider
Rotate any exposed API keys after review

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Aider has unrestricted filesystem write and modify_git_state in a shared git repo, while Plane can also handle files and broad network egress. Even though Plane is not writable locally, Aider's default git commits can race with other repo users or automation, and the shared-state model makes conflicting edits likely. Uncertainty about Plane's deployment model pushes this to high rather than medium.
conditions: IF both agents operate on the same git repository or mirrored work items
IF Plane-generated file exports are later committed by Aider without locking
mitigations: Assign one agent as the sole writer per repo path
Pause Plane exports during Aider commit windows
Use branch-per-agent workflows
Add a lock file or merge gate before commits
requires-engineering: implement optimistic concurrency checks

D_cascading_error.rationale: Aider can generate code changes and commit them, and Plane can store tasks, notes, and roadmaps that may be treated as authoritative downstream. If Plane consumes Aider-produced summaries without verification, errors can cascade into task tracking or scheduling decisions. The pair does not prove automatic action-taking, so medium fits the documented but indirect pathway.
conditions: IF Plane users copy Aider-generated summaries into issues without review
IF Aider commits code based on unverified task text from Plane
mitigations: Require human review of Aider outputs before issue creation
Tag Aider-generated text as unverified in Plane
Compare commits against task acceptance criteria
Use checklists for any task-to-code handoff

E_compliance.rationale: Both profiles are open-source and show no explicit residency, certification, or retention mismatch. Aider handles model-provider API keys and code, while Plane handles issues, files, and notes, but the profiles do not document a compliance conflict. Because the evidence is sparse, I keep this low rather than none, but the other agent is not separately cited for a specific violation.
conditions: IF the deployment stores regulated data in Plane without a matching retention policy
IF Aider is configured to process regulated code or secrets under a stricter policy than Plane
mitigations: Document data-class handling for both tools
Keep regulated data out of Plane uploads
Review retention settings before rollout
Separate environments for sensitive and non-sensitive work
